newsitem.title: USA: Top execs blast SEC, FASB haste in accounting rules.
newsitem.headline: Top execs blast SEC, FASB haste in accounting rules.

text.p: A group of top executives on Thursday criticized the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Financial Accounting Standards Board for pushing ahead quickly on controversial derivatives accounting rules.

The group, which includes former deputy Treasury Secretary Frank Newman who is now the chairman, chief executive and president of Bankers Trust New York Corp, warned SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt and FASB Chairman Edmund Jenkins, against moving forward with the hedge accounting rules without seeking more industry input.

"The FASB may not have adequately considered the wide range of concerns that have been expressed about the derivatives and hedging proposal, including concerns related to the potential impact on the capital markets, the weakening of companies' ability to manage risk and the adverse control implications," the executives wrote in a July 31 letter.

The group, which also includes Federal National Mortgage Association chairman and CEO James Johnson, said FASB, the SEC, other federal regulatory agencies and Congress should consider these issues before finalizing the rules.

"We understand the desire to bring this process to a prompt conclusion, but the underlying issues are so important to this nation's businesses, the customers they serve and the economy as a whole that expediency cannot be the dominant consideration," the group wrote.

The group's concerns come after the accounting standards setting board earlier this month opted to move ahead with a final rule on the accounting of derivatives used as a hedge against the wishes of key market players and some top lawmakers.

Although certain issues remain to be resolved, the basic approach to the rules is to require that all derivatives be recognized in the financial statement. Gains and losses resulting from changes in fair values would be accounted for depending on the use of the derivative.

Other top executives who signed the letter include: Alex J. Pollock, president and chief executive officer of the Federal Home Loan Bank of Chicago; Edward Crutchfield, chairman and CEO of First Union Corp ; William Christ, CFO and treasury of Hershey Foods Corp ; Leland Brendsel, chairman and CEO of the Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp ; and John Reed, chairman of Citicorp.
